title: What the 2026 Midterm Election Results Mean for U.S. Refugee Policy
subtitle: What a new Congress could change in refugee funding and admissions, and which decisions remain with the president.

content.text: With the 2026 midterms over, we think it’s time to look at current refugee policies and what the election results could change.

Before the election results were announced, FiftyPlusOne predicted on November 3rd that Democrats had a 99% chance of winning the House of Representatives and a 79% chance of winning the Senate. These figures refer to which party gains a majority of seats, not the Democratic vote share.

The Associated Press announced the Democratic victory in the Senate on November 3rd and in the House the following day. The new congressional term begins on January 3, 2027. However, the next federal funding decision will still be handled by the outgoing Congress. The current temporary funding law is valid until December 11th unless the corresponding funding is replaced by a new law earlier.

This gives Democrats the opportunity to amend laws, decide on funding, and conduct committee investigations. Trump remains president and can still veto bills. Annual admission caps, orders suspending entry, and funding to support related work each have their own legal basis. They need to be addressed separately.

content.text: Who decides the 17,500-person cap?

On September 25, 2026, the President capped refugee admissions for fiscal year 2027 at 17,500, primarily allocating places to Afrikaners from South Africa. This cap allows the government to accept this many people without requiring it to use all available places.

Section 207 of the Immigration and Nationality Act puts the annual cap in the president’s hands, “after appropriate consultation” with Congress. Cabinet-level representatives must meet members of the House and Senate Judiciary committees in person. Discussions must cover refugee needs, quota allocation, and costs. This process provides Congress with an opportunity to question and exert pressure, but does not grant the Judiciary committees the power to approve or veto the cap. Changing the committee will not automatically alter the September 25 decision.

The suspension of admissions is based on other grounds. Section 212(f) allows the President to restrict the entry of certain categories of aliens when he determines that their entry is detrimental to U.S. interests. Executive Order 14163 invokes this power, listing considerations including national security, reception capacity, resources, social integration, and the responsibilities of state and local governments. The Secretary of State and the Secretary of Homeland Security can jointly approve individual exceptions at their discretion, provided that entry is in the national interest and does not threaten U.S. security or well-being.

The president can also raise the cap during their term. Biden invoked Section 207(b) emergency powers on May 3, 2021, raising the annual cap from 15,000 to 62,500. Trump invoked the same provision on May 21, 2026, raising the fiscal year 2026 cap from 7,500 to 17,500, allocating the additional seats to Afrikaners. Congress can request further adjustments from the president; mandating a cap increase requires new legislation. This is a different path from a president making a voluntary new decision.
December Appropriations Decision

The December 11 deadline leaves different options for the new and old Congresses. The current Congress can pass full-year appropriations or extend the temporary funding. If the new deadline falls after January 3rd, the next decision may go to the new Democratic-controlled Congress; if a full-year plan is passed now, further spending for fiscal year 2027 will be determined before the Democrats take over.

The temporary funding law essentially continues the amounts and conditions of fiscal year 2026 and restricts the initiation or resumption of projects without corresponding fiscal year 2026 appropriations, funding, or authorization. To expand refugee claim processing, lawmakers need to clarify which account the money will come from, what it can be used for, and which restrictions require exceptions. December 11th is not a uniform due date for all refugee-related funding. Different accounts and funding deadlines still need to be reviewed separately.

A majority of seats makes it easier for Democrats to schedule hearings and push through legislation. However, a bill still needs to pass both houses of Congress before being sent to the president for signature. If Trump vetoes it, a two-thirds majority in both houses is needed to override the veto. Democrats could win the election but still lack those votes.

The Senate faces another hurdle. Ending debate on an ordinary bill typically requires a three-fifths majority vote of senators duly chosen and sworn, usually 60 votes. The vote to end debate is different from the vote to pass the bill. Simply counting those who support a bill may overlook situations where it never even makes it to the final vote.

Lawmakers can restrict the use of funds in appropriations laws or directly amend refugee admissions laws. The former applies to designated funds during the periods stated in the law; the latter can change rules that continue to apply. Therefore, proposals need to specify which power or obligation is being changed. Simply increasing the budget does not eliminate the president's statutory power to suspend entry.
What answers can Congress demand?

Even if a new bill doesn't immediately have enough votes, Congress has readily available oversight mechanisms. Section 207(d) requires the government to submit a report on the global refugee situation and admission proposals before the start of each fiscal year and to regularly discuss progress and quota adjustments with the Judiciary committees. Section 207(e) lists the information required for consultations, including country of origin, costs, impact on the United States, and participation from other countries. The annual proposal must also be reviewed at a hearing unless public disclosure would jeopardize lives or safety. New committee chairs can use these existing requirements to question specific decisions.

A specific issue is how the quotas are allocated. Congress can require the government to explain why Afrikaners are prioritized, what evidence was used in assessing other groups, and how these choices meet the legal definition of refugee. Reviewing this basis does not presume that people of a particular nationality are inherently eligible or ineligible.

Exceptions to the suspension order can also be reviewed separately. How many requests has the government received? How many have been approved? How many have actually arrived? Breaking these figures down by month and processing stage can show where delays occurred while protecting sensitive information in individual files. Those still awaiting travel arrangements after approval should not be counted as having arrived.

Refugee admissions should also be distinguished from asylum applications. Under Section 208, those already in the U.S. or at the border can apply for asylum under the conditions and restrictions stipulated by law. Asylum decisions made under Section 208 do not count against the refugee admission quotas under Section 207. Adding the two sets of figures together does not indicate whether the annual admission cap has been enforced and can obscure which law needs to be amended.

In its March 5, 2026 decision in Pacito v. Trump, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals reviewed appeals from preliminary injunctions against the government. The court recognized the president's broad powers in suspending refugee admissions and overturned parts of the injunction concerning admissions, processing, and overseas funding. The ruling also interpreted Section 207 as a cap on admissions, rather than a minimum required. This was a preliminary relief ruling and did not close the case.

Therefore, lawmakers hoping to restore refugee admissions may need to address the relationship between Section 207 and Section 212(f), as well as the specific obligations the government bears in processing applications. Exceptions, time limits, and judicial review may also need to be included in the plan. Otherwise, even with an increased annual cap, the existing entry restrictions may still apply.
